raw_response:
I've been farming this same land in Quzhou for over forty years. My father farmed it before me, and his father before him. I know this soil. I know what it wants.

The land is flat. The water table keeps dropping — the well pump has to work harder every year, and the neighbors say the same. But I do what I have always done. There is no reason to change what has worked.

**Winter wheat first.** I plant in October, just as the weather turns cold. I buy the improved seed from the county supply cooperative — the same variety I've used for the past several years, 济麦22 or something similar. I don't trust the new experimental kinds. Too much risk for a man my age with only 5 mu. I'll plough the field properly before planting, the way my father taught me. Fertilizer goes in at planting and again at jointing. I irrigate four times: before winter sets in, at green-up in spring, at jointing, and at grain fill. I've seen what happens when you skip the jointing irrigation — the yield drops badly. Two pesticide sprays: one herbicide early on, one fungicide when I see rust starting to show on the leaves.

**Summer maize follows immediately after wheat harvest in June.** I rotary-till just enough to break up the stubble. No time to plough properly — maize seed goes in fast so the plants can use the summer rains. I buy hybrid seed,郑单958 style — everyone around here does. The summer rains usually handle most of the water. I'll irrigate once if August turns dry. Mainly I spray herbicide once early and check for corn borer. By late September I harvest.

That is my year. Wheat and maize. Always has been.
